REAL ESTATE BROKER AND SALESPERSON LICENSING LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe Realty, Inc. · John Smith

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law on who must hold a real estate license to act as a real estate broker or real estate salesperson, Business and Professions Code section 10130 et seq. It is prepared with reference to Jane Doe Realty, Inc. as broker and, if applicable, John Smith as salesperson. This sheet is separate from, and covers different subject matter than, a Real Estate Agency Relationship Disclosure: that document addresses the fiduciary duties an already-licensed agent owes to a buyer or seller once an agency relationship exists in a transaction, while this sheet addresses a threshold question that comes before any agency relationship — the statutory licensing requirement itself, who the statute defines as needing a broker's license, how a salesperson's license differs from a broker's license, and the statute's own stated consequences for engaging in licensed real estate activity without a license. This sheet does not determine whether Jane Doe Realty, Inc. or John Smith holds a current, valid license, does not evaluate whether any particular activity requires a license, and does not tell any person what to do about their own licensing status.

BASIC LICENSING REQUIREMENT
California law makes it unlawful for any person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within the state without first obtaining a real estate license from the Department of Real Estate. The same section separately makes it unlawful to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a mortgage loan originator without having obtained a license endorsement. The statute assigns the Real Estate Commissioner a role in bringing a complaint for a violation, and it makes it the duty of the district attorney of each county to prosecute violations occurring in that county.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "It is unlawful for any person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within this state without first obtaining a real estate license from the department, or to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a mortgage loan originator within this state without having obtained a license endorsement."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10130 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10130 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10130.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general licensing requirement itself; it does not state what activities count as acting as a broker or salesperson (a separate clause addresses the statutory definition), does not describe the statute's own exemptions from the requirement (also addressed separately), and does not itself determine whether any particular person's conduct falls within or outside the licensing requirement.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF ACTIVITIES REQUIRING A BROKER'S LICENSE
California law defines a real estate broker, for purposes of the licensing chapter, as a person who does or negotiates to do, for another or others and for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, one or more of a defined list of acts: selling, buying, or soliciting or obtaining listings for the sale, purchase, or exchange of real property or a business opportunity; leasing or renting real property or a business opportunity, soliciting tenants or rental listings, negotiating leases, or collecting rents; assisting in filing an application to purchase or lease, or to locate or enter upon, land owned by the state or federal government; soliciting borrowers or lenders, negotiating loans, or collecting payments or performing services for borrowers, lenders, or note owners on loans secured by real property or a business opportunity; and selling, buying, or exchanging a real property sales contract or a note secured by a lien on real property or a business opportunity, and performing services for the holders of such a contract or note. The statute contains several additional sections extending the broker definition to other specific activities, such as certain loan and mineral-, oil-, or gas-property transactions, that this clause does not separately catalog.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A real estate broker within the meaning of this part is a person who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, regardless of the form or time of payment, does or negotiates to do one or more of the following acts for another or others: (a) Sells or offers to sell, buys or offers to buy, solicits prospective sellers or buyers of, solicits or obtains listings of, or negotiates the purchase, sale, or exchange of real property or a business opportunity."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10131 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10131 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10131.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Business and Professions Code section 10131; it does not quote the several adjoining sections (10131.01 through 10131.7) that extend the broker definition to additional specific activities, such as advance-fee listing arrangements, securities transactions described in the Corporations Code, and mineral, oil, or gas property, nor does it address the statutory exemptions from the licensing requirement, which are addressed in a separate clause. It also does not determine whether any specific act by any particular person falls within this definition.

BROKER LICENSE VERSUS SALESPERSON LICENSE
California law defines these as two distinct license types with a defined relationship to each other. A "real estate broker" is a person licensed as a broker. A "real estate salesperson" is a natural person licensed as a salesperson who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, is retained by a real estate broker to perform one or more of the acts that require a real estate license. A salesperson's license is thus defined by statute as operating through, and by retention of, a licensed broker, rather than as an independent authorization to act on one's own.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Real estate broker” means a person licensed as a broker under Chapter 3 of this part."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10015 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10015 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10015.)
  "“Real estate salesperson” means a natural person licensed as a salesperson under Chapter 3 of this part and who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, is retained by a real estate broker to do one or more of the acts set forth in Sections 10131, 10131.1, 10131.2, 10131.3, 10131.4, and 10131.6."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10016 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10016 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10016.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statutory definitions of the two license types; it does not itself state every statutory consequence that follows from a salesperson's license being tied to a broker (the compensation-flow and supervision rules are addressed in a separate clause), and it does not determine whether any particular salesperson's retention by any particular broker, or any other arrangement between them, satisfies these definitions.

COMPENSATION MUST FLOW THROUGH THE EMPLOYING BROKER
Consistent with a salesperson's license being tied to a specific broker, the statute makes it unlawful for a licensed broker to retain or compensate any person for performing licensed activity who is not a licensed broker or a salesperson licensed under that same responsible broker. It further provides that no salesperson may accept compensation for activity requiring a real estate license from anyone other than the broker under whom the salesperson is at the time licensed, and makes it unlawful for a salesperson to pay compensation for such activity to any real estate licensee except through that broker; two licensees may agree to share compensation only if it is paid through the responsible broker. Separately, the statute assigns the officer designated by a corporate broker licensee responsibility for supervision and control of the salespersons licensed to that corporation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No real estate salesperson shall accept compensation for activity requiring a real estate license from any person other than the broker under whom he or she is at the time licensed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10137 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10137 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10137.)
  "The officer designated by a corporate broker licensee pursuant to Section 10211 shall be responsible for the supervision and control of the activities conducted on behalf of the corporation by its officers and employees as necessary to secure full compliance with the provisions of this division, including the supervision of salespersons licensed to the corporation in the performance of acts for which a real estate license is required."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10159.2(a) (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10159.2(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10159.2.)
  Known gap: This clause addresses the compensation-flow rule of section 10137 and the corporate-broker supervision rule of section 10159.2; it does not address every other statutory supervision duty a broker owes with respect to a salesperson's conduct, and it does not determine whether any particular broker's or salesperson's actual compensation arrangement complies with this rule.

STATUTORY EXEMPTIONS FROM THE LICENSE REQUIREMENT
The statute lists categories of persons for whom the acts described in the broker definition are not acts requiring a real estate license: a regular corporate officer or general partner acting for the corporation or partnership's own owned or leased property, if not acting for special compensation; a person holding a duly executed power of attorney from the property owner; an attorney at law rendering legal services to a client; a receiver, bankruptcy trustee, or other person acting under court order; and a trustee under a deed of trust selling under that deed of trust's authority. The statute itself states that these exemptions do not apply to a person who uses or attempts to use them to evade the licensing requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The acts described in Section 10131 are not acts for which a real estate license is required if performed by: (1) A regular officer of a corporation or a general partner of a partnership with respect to real property owned or leased by the corporation or partnership, respectively, or in connection with the proposed purchase or leasing of real property by the corporation or partnership, respectively, if the acts are not performed by the officer or partner in expectation of special compensation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10133 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10133 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10133.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the exemption list in section 10133; the statute contains a separate, more detailed exemption scheme (section 10133.1 and related sections) for loan-related and lender-affiliated activity that this clause does not cover, and this sheet does not determine whether any exemption applies to any particular person's actual conduct.

BAR ON SUING TO COLLECT COMPENSATION WITHOUT A LICENSE
The statute bars a person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a real estate broker or real estate salesperson from bringing or maintaining any action in the courts of this state to collect compensation for performing any of the licensed acts, unless that person alleges and proves that they were a duly licensed real estate broker or real estate salesperson at the time the cause of action arose. Because this pleading-and-proof requirement is a precondition to maintaining the action at all, it is the statutory basis on which unlicensed status has been raised as a defense to a claim for a real estate commission.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within this state shall bring or maintain any action in the courts of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any of the acts mentioned in this article without alleging and proving that he or she was a duly licensed real estate broker or real estate salesperson at the time the alleged cause of action arose."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10136 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10136 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10136.)
  Known gap: This clause is confined to what section 10136 itself provides — a bar on maintaining a court action absent alleged and proved licensure at the time the claim arose. It does not address how courts have applied this rule to particular fact patterns (for example, substantial-compliance or licensing-at-time-of-suit arguments), since that requires case law this document does not independently verify here (a CourtListener case law search for this topic returned a quota-exceeded error at the time this sheet was prepared, so no case law is cited). This clause also does not determine whether any particular broker or salesperson was licensed at any particular time.

CRIMINAL PENALTY FOR UNLICENSED ACTIVITY
Separately from the bar on collecting compensation through the courts, the statute makes it a public offense for any person to act as a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without a license or license endorsement, or to advertise using words indicating that they are one of these without being so licensed or endorsed. The statute sets the penalty at a fine not exceeding $20,000, imprisonment in the county jail for not more than six months, or both, or, for a corporation, a fine not exceeding $60,000.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any person acting as a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without a license or license endorsement, or who advertises using words indicating that he or she is a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without being so licensed or without having obtained a license endorsement, shall be guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or by imprisonment in the county jail for a term not to exceed six months, or by both fine and imprisonment; or if a corporation, be punished by a fine not exceeding sixty thousand dollars ($60,000)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10139 (leginfo text), Business and Professions Code § 10139 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=10139.)
  Known gap: This clause states the criminal penalty provision itself; it does not address how or whether it has been enforced in any particular circumstance, and it is separate from the civil consequence described in the compensation-bar clause (section 10136), which does not require a criminal conviction.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet was prepared for reference concerning Jane Doe Realty, Inc. and, if applicable, John Smith, and does not itself constitute a license, a determination of licensing status, or legal advice about compliance with Business and Professions Code section 10130 et seq. Prepared and reviewed as of January 1, 2026, at Sacramento, California.
